one_liner: Small MIT C++20 in-place WebAssembly interpreter: validate and run bytecode directly, starting large modules about 5x faster than Wasmtime.
what_it_does: Loads a Wasm binary, validates every function eagerly, and interprets the original bytecode without translating it. API: mitey::Module::compile(std::unique_ptr<uint8_t[]>, length) returns a shared_ptr<Module>; module->instantiate(imports) gives an Instance whose get_exports() entries convert to typed C++ callables (FunctionInfo::to<float()>()), and host functions are wrapped with wasm_functionify. It is a library-shaped hobby runtime, not a drop-in for Wasmtime's API or CLI, and it ships no WASI layer.
how_it_is_fast: Startup is cheap because there is no compile step: one validation pass per function records branch targets in side tables (std::unordered_map from block/if bytecode address to its end or else position), in the style of Ben Titzer's in-place interpreter, and instantiation only allocates stacks and copies those tables. Dispatch is a 256-entry handler table with [[clang::musttail]] tail calls between handlers (threaded code without computed goto), the hot state (instance, bytecode pointer, value stack, control stack) travels in argument registers, and cold paths such as multi-value branch moves and error raising are noinline preserve_most functions.
when_to_use: Short-lived invocations of large modules where compile latency dominates and little code runs (author's numbers on an M1: SpiderMonkey module up and instantiated in 35.4 ms vs 183.3 ms for Wasmtime).

Reading or vendoring a compact, MIT-licensed C++ example of an in-place Wasm interpreter with tail-call dispatch (about 4,300 lines in six source files: module.cpp, instance.cpp, main.cpp and three headers).
Embedding pure-compute modules with a few custom host imports (no WASI) in a C++ program where portability of plain C++20 matters more than speed.
when_not_to_use: Any compute-heavy run: the author's numbers put it at Coremark 749.6 vs 28260.4 for Wasmtime (about 38x slower), SpiderMonkey score about 2.83 vs 577, and esbuild too slow to report.
Programs that need WASI, SIMD (v128 is commented out in spec.hpp), threads or 64-bit memories: none are implemented.
Deeply recursive code: the control stack holds 1000 entries (MAX_DEPTH) shared by every active call and every entered block, after which it traps 'call stack exhausted'.
Production use: stale since 2025-07-15, 6 stars, README is a single heading with no documentation, and the very largest binary (Figma) starts faster under Node (92.5 vs 108.3 ms).

integration.dependencies: none (C++ standard library only); the spec-test runner needs wast2json and Python 3
integration.min_toolchain: C++20; the Makefile uses clang++ and warns that Clang 15 and below have incomplete C++20 support; dispatch relies on [[clang::musttail]] (the Makefile passes -Wno-attributes, so a compiler that ignores the attribute loses the tail-call guarantee); commits mention GCC fixes
integration.platforms: Not documented; plain C++20 with no OS-specific calls seen, but uses POSIX ssize_t; memory is calloc/realloc with explicit bounds checks, 32-bit addresses only
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. Each Instance owns its value stack, control stack and mutable call frame, so use one thread per Instance; no shared mutable globals were seen apart from read-only handler tables.

gotchas: Build-file flaw: plain make builds the debug target (-Og -g3 -DWASM_DEBUG -fsanitize=address,undefined; WASM_DEBUG prints every executed instruction and the stack to stderr), and 'make release' fails with "No rule to make target 'release'" because release only carries a target-specific -O2 (checked with make -n). An optimized build needs something like make executable CFLAGS="-std=c++20 -O2"; which build the blog numbers used is unknown.

The published driver cannot reproduce the post's startup numbers: main.cpp supplies only env.clock_ms and calls an export named 'run' (a Coremark-style driver), and there is no WASI code in the repo, so the SpiderMonkey, esbuild and Figma binaries would stop at an 'unknown import' link error during instantiation. The harness used for the post is not public.

Each executed block and if does a std::unordered_map lookup keyed by bytecode address, and loop re-decodes its blocktype on every iteration; every Instance deep-copies both maps from the Module, so instantiation cost and memory grow with the number of blocks.

Linear memory is calloc/realloc'd (grow copies; calloc failure is not checked) and the bounds check computes current * PAGE_SIZE in 32 bits, so a memory at the full 65536 pages wraps to 0 and every access traps. Traps and validation failures are C++ exceptions (trap_error, validation_error, link_error).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: For startup alone, Wasmi with lazy translation and the DLR-FT wasm-interpreter have independent wasmi-benchmarks numbers and are maintained, and wasm3 or WAMR's fast interpreter are far faster at execution; pick this one only when you want a small MIT C++ in-place interpreter to read or vendor, with your own host imports and no WASI.
verified_claims_summary: Author's own blog post (csjh.blog, blocked here; numbers relayed by search snippets) timed load+validate+instantiate with hyperfine on an M1 MacBook Air: SpiderMonkey 35.4 ms vs Wasmtime 183.3 ms, Wasmtime single-pass 197.4 ms and Node 66.3 ms; esbuild 64.7 vs 209.9 ms (Node 75.3); Figma 108.3 vs 710.4 ms (Node 92.5, faster). Validation alone is 24.8 ms on SpiderMonkey; compiler flags, the driver used and Wasmtime's cache settings are not known, and execution is 38x or more slower than Wasmtime.
status_note: Stale (244 commits, last a merged saturating-truncate fix on 2025-07-15; the author's later work is mitey-jit) but MIT-licensed and small enough to vendor; no documentation, no WASI, and the Makefile's release target is broken.
